content:
Multiple Dropbox users have received emails from the cloud storage company notifying them that their accounts were accessed without authorization due to a security vulnerability.

The root cause appears to be Dropbox's lack of an authentication process when attackers set up single sign-on (SSO) options through third-party companies……

Developer Yoni Levy shared the contents of the email he received on the social platform X.

Other Dropbox users also reported receiving similar emails, which mentioned that the incident was due to issues with the single sign-on (SSO) option when using Lenovo ID.

However, while Dropbox claims the vulnerability lies in Lenovo's email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to verify the new single sign-on setup through their original login method, as reported by The CyberSec Guru.

  • Reconnaissance and filtering: Attackers collect target email addresses (through leaked databases, LinkedIn, customer lists—email addresses are essentially public information).
  • Malicious identity provider registration: Attackers register a Lenovo ID with victim@example.com. There is no need to access the victim's email during this process, because Lenovo's verification steps are either missing or can be bypassed. The display name is set to a disposable name—one of the users who recovered a hijacked account found the name to be the late NFL broadcaster "John Madden," which strongly suggests a bulk, low-cost registration operation.
  • Federated login: The attacker clicks "Continue with Lenovo" on Dropbox. Lenovo's authorization server issues a token, with the email claim matching the victim's Dropbox account.
  • Implicit account linking: Dropbox matches the email claim to the existing account and generates a login session. No password required, no additional verification, and no "Link this new identity?" consent prompt. For Dropbox, a trusted identity provider has already vouched for that email address.

9to5Mac's take

Although there are indeed shortcomings on Lenovo's side regarding email address verification, if Dropbox had authenticated the linked identity before it was used to log in, no harm would have been done at all. The failure to do so is a serious oversight.

The company has since fixed the vulnerability and invalidated all previously "authenticated" sessions through Lenovo ID.
